case40v1-val.concierge:
Indian School of Business · Software Product Management · Case

Seyal Commerce Technologies: The Desk, The Model and The Dubai Contract

For class discussion. Seyal, Saravai Supermarts, Sankalan Capital and Sanchalan Business Services are fictional; the market and institutions around them are real.

1. Sunday night, Chennai

On the evening of Sunday, 11 October 2026, Darshini Kandaswamy sat on the floor of her flat in Besant Nagar with the six printed exhibits around her and a board deck rewritten twice. The board of Seyal Commerce Technologies met at three the next afternoon; item four read, in her chief executive's clipped idiom, Autopilot: go / no-go.

Seyal sold a deceptively simple service. Once a week, for each of its 1,120 live stores, somebody decided what it should buy, from which distributor and in what quantity, and sent the list to the owner's phone before six on order morning. Owners called it the list. Internally it was the Desk: twenty-five people on a rented floor in Coimbatore, called temporary in every document for nineteen months.

Darshini had joined as vice-president of product fourteen months earlier, from a payments company, and had since been handed the sentence she could not get out of her head: the January 2026 investor update called Seyal's ordering engine AI-driven. It was not false the way a lie is false. A model existed. It simply did not write the lists.

2. How Seyal came to be run by hand

Seyal was founded in 2022 by Deeptanshu Kothapalli and two classmates to sell inventory software to kirana stores in Tamil Nadu and Kerala. It failed in the ordinary way: owners would not key in their stock. In early 2025, with eight months of cash left, Deeptanshu decided that instead of making owners do the work, Seyal would do it for them by hand, for as long as it took to understand the job.

On Monday, 17 March 2025, Seyal opened a twelve-seat floor in Coimbatore under contract with Sanchalan Business Services and began producing order lists by hand. Retention went from poor to remarkable. Stores paid. By October 2025 Sankalan Capital led a ₹46 crore Series A.

Two features of that decision constrain October 2026. The first is commercial: for a preferential rate, Seyal signed a thirty-six-month agreement with Sanchalan for thirty seats to 31 March 2028, terminable on six months' notice with a ₹1.1 crore exit fee before 30 September 2027. The second is epistemic, and worse. The Desk was built to deliver lists, not to record how they were decided: analysts reasoned in WhatsApp threads, calls and a spreadsheet, and only the finished list was stored. Seyal ran what a textbook would call a concierge test for nineteen months, kept the output and discarded the reasoning. A structured why-field arrived only with the pilot, completed for 6,100 of the pilot's 6,240 weekly lists (98 per cent).

3. The industry

India's small-format grocery trade was, in 2026, under pressure from two directions. Quick-commerce — Zepto, Blinkit, Swiggy Instamart — had taken the top-up basket in metros. Udaan, ElasticRun, Jumbotail and Reliance Retail's cash-and-carry operations competed for the kirana's supply side. ONDC had made catalogue and order flows between unaffiliated buyers and sellers ordinary; UPI, on NPCI rails, made payment trivial. What remained hard was how much of which pack size a 320-square-foot store in Tiruppur should buy on a Tuesday in Margazhi.

Regulation touched Seyal at three points. GST e-invoicing on its distributor partners drove an integration occupying two Pune engineers until 31 January 2027. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 governed the consent under which Seyal held WhatsApp-sourced store data, refresh due 31 March 2027. Export exposure arrived as Saravai Supermarts, a forty-one-store Indian-origin grocery chain in the UAE, whose group chief information officer in Dubai, Dinkar Kodandaraman, offered a three-year licence worth about ₹4.9 crore, roughly ₹1.63 crore a year, on one condition: store-level data stays in the UAE, with no operational access from India. The Desk could not serve Saravai. Only a model could.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

By April 2026 Seyal billed 820 stores and the Desk was thought a bridge automation would retire. On Friday, 19 June 2026, Devdutt Koneru's team circulated a charter for Seyal Autopilot — model-generated lists, analysts reviewing only exceptions — promising a representative sample of 240 stores against 240 run as usual. Between Wednesday, 24 June and Friday, 26 June the arms were assigned, by the Desk, from a list it produced itself.

The pilot ran thirteen weeks, Wednesday 1 July to Tuesday 29 September 2026, and its results (Exhibit 4) read as encouraging on cost and worrying on acceptance. What turned out wrong was the word representative. Drishti Kesineni pulled the arms' June baselines in August and found them plainly unalike (Exhibit 5): the Autopilot arm was older, larger, better catalogued, more urban. She filed it on Friday, 14 August 2026 as a comment on the pilot document. Two people opened it.

Three further things have turned out wrong, and they do not point the same way. First, the Desk is not the drag the April plan assumed: ₹112.0 lakh for the six months to 30 September 2026 is ₹18.7 lakh a month against net burn averaging ₹184 lakh a month, about a tenth. Second, it is near a ceiling the Coimbatore contract sets, not one money sets (Exhibit 2). Third, a September survey found a little over half of the owners who answered believe a computer already writes their list (Exhibit 6). Nobody had decided to tell them that; nobody had decided not to, either.

5. The people

Darshini Kandaswamy, vice-president of product, Chennai. Owns the recommendation, and says the pilot answered a narrower question than the board thinks. Incentive: a product team she may grow to eleven once Autopilot ships. Not saying: she suspects the Desk is the product, and that saying so makes her the executive arguing for headcount in Coimbatore, not her own.

Deeptanshu Kothapalli, co-founder and chief executive, Chennai. Made the March 2025 decision, is proud of it, and wants a decision on Monday, not a study. Incentive: a Series B conversation opening February 2027, for which gross margin improving is the required sentence. Not saying: he wrote the January 2026 update.

Dakshayani Karunakaran, head of the Desk, Coimbatore. Twenty-five people through three supervisors. Argues acceptance is the only part of Exhibit 4 that matters: a list a store ignores is worse than none. States her own interest plainly, which disarms people. Not saying: from week nine her supervisors were quietly correcting Autopilot lists where they expected trouble.

Devdutt Koneru, head of engineering, Bengaluru. Nine there, five in Pune. Holds that Autopilot clears the cost bar and acceptance is a tuning problem. Incentive: three quarters of building, and two engineers who will leave if it is shelved. Not saying: v2 needs eleven engineer-months he lacks until the GST work ends on 31 January 2027.

Drishti Kesineni, lead data scientist, Toronto. The only person outside the Desk who has read the assignment log. Position: the pilot cannot estimate Autopilot's effect on anything, because the arms differ. Incentive: methodological reputation. Not saying: a clean test needs a quarter Seyal cannot spare, uncosted.

Dipesh Kolipaka, principal designer, Berlin. Designed the store app. Position: Exhibit 6 is a design failure he caused and should fix. Not saying: he has drafted a screen naming the analyst behind each list, unshown to Dakshayani, whose team it would name.

Dhrupad Kalyanasundaram, head of sales, Edison, New Jersey. Sells to Indian-origin grocery groups in the US and the Gulf; sourced Saravai. Position: sign it, because a licence is worth more than a service. Incentive: his largest commission of the year. Not saying: two of his three US prospects have asked the same data-residency question.

Damayanti Kavuri, customer success lead, Singapore. Ran the September survey. Position: owners who know a person writes their list behave differently from those who think it software, and Seyal should learn why first. Incentive: her retention number. Not saying: she wrote the question herself, in English over WhatsApp, and is unsure what a computer at Seyal meant in Palakkad.

6. Exhibits

Across the 5,820 store-months in Exhibit 2, ₹112.0 lakh is ₹1,924 a store-month against a subscription of ₹1,450. On average a store loses ₹474 a month before an engineer is paid, the number Deeptanshu quotes.

7. Voices

Desk cost is ₹1,924 a store-month. Autopilot takes thirty-four analyst-minutes a week down to nine: over thirteen weeks, 442 minutes a store against 117. At ₹42,000 for 9,000 productive minutes, that is ₹2,063 against ₹546 — ₹1,517 over three months, ₹506 a month. Call it ₹1,418: above water on subscription alone.Devdutt Koneru, engineering review, 5 October 2026
Your ₹506 comes out of the ₹952 of analyst salary inside that ₹1,924, not the whole thing. Supervisors, field team, telephony, tooling and rent are the other ₹972, none of which fall. Escalations went from 412 to 1,886: at eleven supervisor-minutes each and ₹9.44 a minute (₹85,000 over 9,000), ₹59 a store-month on the Desk arm against ₹272 on Autopilot. So ₹506 less ₹213 is ₹293 — fifteen per cent of ₹1,924, not a rescue.Drishti Kesineni, reply on the same thread
Autopilot routed ₹1,034 lakh against the Desk's ₹961 lakh — ₹73 lakh more, and at the contractual 0.605 per cent that is ₹44,165, or ₹61 a store-month better.Devdutt Koneru, follow-up
Autopilot's stores had median monthly purchases of ₹1.46 lakh, the Desk's ₹1.18 lakh. A bigger wallet routed more rupees. That is the arms differing, not the model working, and the pilot cannot say what Autopilot does to routed value in either direction. The two measures whose bias runs against the model are acceptance and churn — the easier arm did worse on both — and neither is easy to dismiss.Drishti Kesineni, same thread
Saravai is ₹4.9 crore. Our entire India book did ₹140 lakh in six months. This is nearly twice the company.Dhrupad Kalyanasundaram, sales call, 7 October 2026
₹4.9 crore is three years: ₹1.63 crore a year against ₹2.44 crore if India merely holds, twice the half-year's recurring ₹121.8 lakh. About two-thirds of India's revenue, Dhrupad, not twice the company — and what matters is that we cannot serve it with people.Darshini Kandaswamy, reply
Fifty-four per cent of the owners who answered think a machine does this. My analyst calls a store in Erode every Thursday because the owner's son orders that day and gets it wrong. Which fact goes in the app?Dakshayani Karunakaran, operations review, 9 October 2026

8. The options as Darshini sees them

A. Ship Autopilot. Roll out from 1 January 2027, cut the Desk to twelve exception handlers, give Sanchalan notice on 31 March 2027 to clear the ₹1.1 crore exit fee, sign Saravai. Gross margin improves in the Series B deck; the acceptance gap is a tuning problem.

B. Keep the Desk and price for it. Raise the subscription from ₹1,450 to ₹2,200 on sixty days' notice, grow to the Sanchalan ceiling of about 1,650 stores, decline Saravai, and tell the board the engine is people. Recurring contribution is ₹168 a store-month today; the ₹750 rise would take it to ₹918, if nobody leaves.

C. Split the book. Autopilot for stores with clean data, the Desk for the rest. Across the book 426 of 1,120 stores (38 per cent) have twelve months or more of digitised invoices, against 201 of 240 (84 per cent) in the Autopilot arm.

D. Instrument first. Spend the December quarter capturing how analysts decide, then automate against that. Misses Saravai's deadline, and means telling the board the January 2026 update described something that does not exist.

Darshini has written all four down and cannot tell whether the list itself is wrong. All four treat the Desk as a cost to be reduced, retained or repriced; none asks what the stores are buying. The clean data in option C is produced by the Desk, so automating the clean stores first may starve the next cohort — or may not. And the pilot ran two questions together: whether a model can write a good list, and whether Seyal knows what a good list is. Dipesh's unshown screen might be a fifth option, or a distraction.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

Cash at 30 September 2026 was ₹28.6 crore. Net burn over the six months to that date totalled ₹11.04 crore, ₹1.84 crore a month: a little over fifteen months from 30 September 2026 at that rate. Seyal's payroll and contracted floor together run to sixty-three people, and the Toronto and Berlin salaries alone — CAD 165,000 and EUR 105,000, or ₹1.02 crore and ₹97.65 lakh a year at ₹62 and ₹93 — come to ₹16.66 lakh a month against ₹11.79 lakh of loaded cost for all twenty-five in Coimbatore, about 1.4 times as much.

The Sanchalan agreement runs to 31 March 2028: thirty seats, six months' notice, ₹1.1 crore to exit before 30 September 2027. Autopilot v2 needs eleven engineer-months, and two of the five Pune engineers are on GST e-invoicing until 31 January 2027. DPDP consent refresh is due by 31 March 2027. Saravai must be signed by Tuesday, 15 December 2026, ₹1.2 crore on signature, and its policy forbids Indian operational access to store-level data. A price change requires sixty days' notice. And Dharitri Kattamuri of Sankalan Capital, on the board, wants a decision at Monday's meeting, not a plan to decide.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. What did nineteen months of delivering the list by hand teach Seyal, and where is that learning stored? What was discarded, and what would keeping it have cost?
  2. Exhibits 1 and 3 point in opposite directions on the same six months. Which is the right base for a decision about the Desk, and what does the ₹18.2 lakh footnote do to it?
  3. What would have to be true of Exhibit 4 for it to support a rollout? Design the comparison you would have run in June 2026, within Seyal's constraints.
  4. A little over half of the owners who answered believe a computer writes their list. What does that create, and to whom: the stores, the board, Saravai, the analysts?
  5. Darshini's four options all treat the Desk as a cost. What option is missing, what would keeping it open a quarter cost, and what would Seyal stop doing to afford it?
  6. It is Monday morning, 12 October 2026, and the board meets at three. What does Darshini do before then, and what exactly does she say to Dharitri Kattamuri about the word AI-driven?

Near eleven, Darshini pulled the Coimbatore roster from the shared drive and read the twenty-two names, most met once. Beside each was a column she had never looked at: stores covered. The numbers ran from 38 to 71. Somebody had been making that allocation for nineteen months by a rule nobody had written down, and the model in Bengaluru was trained on the lists it produced, not on the rule.

She looked again at slide four — Autopilot: go / no-go — and thought the honest version had a third box she could not label. Outside, the last Sunday-night autos thinned out on Elliot's Beach Road. She had until three.
case20v1-val.concierge:
Rojmel Works: Hand-Made Before Machine-Made

A decision case on concierge and Wizard of Oz tests

1. Opening

On the morning of Monday, 19 October 2026, Chitralekha Jagannathan, head of product at Rojmel Works, stood at a whiteboard in the company's rented office in T. Nagar, Chennai. On it were two numbers her chief technology officer had written the previous evening: "₹96 lakh" and "5 months". The board would meet on Friday, 23 October, and she had to bring it a single recommendation for how Rojmel should find out whether traders would actually use, and pay for, automatic reconciliation of their purchase bills against the GST portal.

The September GSTR-3B return was due on Tuesday, 20 October. Most of Rojmel's monthly filers would be scrambling over exactly the problem she hoped to solve. She had until Friday to choose between building the engine, delivering the service by hand, or faking the engine convincingly.

2. Company background

Rojmel Works was founded in 2022 by Chiranjeevi Jonnalagadda, a former chartered-accountancy articled clerk from Hyderabad. The name comes from rojmel, the daily cash book that wholesale traders have kept for generations. The company sells a bookkeeping app in Tamil, Telugu and English to wholesale and distribution shops, chiefly in textiles, hardware and grocery, across Tamil Nadu and Telangana. It has 11,500 paying shops at ₹2,400 a year, an annual run-rate of ₹276 lakh, or ₹2.76 crore.

The market is crowded. Vyapar, Khatabook and OkCredit compete for the same shopkeeper's phone, Zoho Books and ClearTax serve the next tier up, and Tally sits on many office desktops. Rojmel's edge has been language and the credit ledger. It has no feature that reconciles input tax credit, the GST a trader has paid on purchases and may claim back, against what suppliers have actually filed with the Goods and Services Tax Network (GSTN). Traders do this by hand, pay an accountant, or skip it and lose credit.

3. The situation

The idea came from support tickets. A trader photographs a supplier's bill on WhatsApp; the system should read it, match it to the trader's auto-drafted statement of purchases (GSTR-2B), and flag mismatches before the return is filed. The CTO, Chezhian Jayakumar in Bengaluru, wants to build it now. His estimate is ₹96 lakh and five months of engineering, about 35 per cent of annual revenue (96 divided by 276).

Chitralekha is less certain, and the discovery work explains why. Between 28 September and 9 October her team interviewed 40 traders in Erode, Hyderabad and Madurai. Exhibit 1 shows that 26 of the 40, or 65.0 per cent, said they would pay ₹600 a month for the service. But this is what traders said, not what they did, and none of the 40 interviewees had been asked to send a bill.

Source: Rojmel discovery interviews, 28 September to 9 October 2026. Share is the count saying yes divided by the count interviewed in that row; the total row is pooled (26 of 40), not a mean of the three rates. Stated intent only; no money changed hands.

In the first fortnight of October, Chiranjeevi and Chitralekha had also quietly processed bills by hand for six friendly traders, none of them among the 40 interviewees. Exhibit 2 records the 300 bills they received. Printed GST invoices took about two and a half minutes each. Handwritten estimate slips, not tax invoices, took six minutes and often could not be matched to anything. Blurred photographs were bounced back.

Average minutes per bill is 950 divided by 300, which is 3.17, shown as 3.2. Six traders over two weeks is 25 bills per trader per week. That is the mean of six hand-picked traders over one fortnight, the run-up to the 20 October return, with no per-trader spread, and the timings exclude supplier phone calls and chasing blurred photos.

Cauvery Jayaraman, the data scientist in Toronto, had separately tested an off-the-shelf reader on 400 printed invoices. All seven key fields were correct on 292 of them, or 73.0 per cent. She had not tested handwritten slips, and she wrote on Slack that she would not expect a usable result.

Chandini Janakiraman, who leads customer success from Singapore, has talked to more traders than anyone. She reported that many traders did not ask for reconciliation at all. They asked "what do I do about this mismatch?", and the answer was often a phone call to the supplier. That step appeared nowhere in the CTO's specification.

4. The people

Chiranjeevi Jonnalagadda, founder and chief executive, Hyderabad. He wants proof the idea is real before the board commits cash, but he also fears looking slow beside better-funded rivals.

Chezhian Jayakumar, chief technology officer, Bengaluru. He wants to build, and he believes manual pilots teach little that engineers could not learn faster from working software.

Chandini Janakiraman, head of customer success, Singapore. She wants to protect trader trust. Traders hand over supplier names and GSTINs, and she is wary of any test that lets them believe a machine, not a person, is reading their books.

Cauvery Jayaraman, data scientist, Toronto. She wants a labelled set of real bills, whatever the route, because she has none beyond the 400 printed invoices.

5. Exhibits and the options

Exhibit 3 sets out three courses of action, built from the figures above. Operators are assumed to cost ₹36,000 a month each. Option B serves 30 traders and Option C serves 120, both at the 25 bills a week of Exhibit 2. That figure is soft. Option B is insensitive to it: 750 bills a week is about 39.6 hours. Option C is not: four operators are exhausted at about 25.3 bills per trader per week, and at 30 it would need five.

Exhibit 3: The three options compared (₹ lakh)
OptionEngineeringOperatorsTools and travelTotalWeeks to first evidence
A. Build the engine96.000.000.0096.0020
B. Concierge, 30 traders0.001.620.382.006
C. Wizard of Oz, 120 traders6.002.881.1210.0012

B: three operators for 1.5 months, more than the roughly 40-hour weekly load needs, to cover onboarding and supplier calls. C: two engineers for four weeks to build a WhatsApp front end, then four operators for two months. Weeks for C include the four-week build. A month is taken as four weeks throughout, so five months is 20 weeks. Weeks are not like-for-like: A is build time only, with no usage afterwards, while B and C include the whole run, though B's payment evidence starts in week 3. The engineering and tools figures are management estimates, not itemised. Weeks to first evidence for A means a working engine in use.

Bar widths: A 20 weeks, B 6 weeks, C 12 weeks, at 20 px per week from the zero line.

Option A: build the engine now. Upside: a finished product, and the CTO's momentum. Cost: ₹96 lakh and 20 weeks before any trader's behaviour is observed, while the handwritten fifth of bills and the supplier-call step remain unaddressed.

Option B: concierge test. Rojmel staff visibly do the reconciliation by hand for 30 chosen traders for six weeks, starting Monday, 26 October. Traders know a person is helping; from week 3, which begins on 9 November, the day after Diwali, they pay ₹600 a month. Upside: low cost, and the team learns the real workflow. Cost: it cannot test speed or the WhatsApp experience.

Option C: Wizard of Oz. Build only a WhatsApp front end that looks automatic while operators work behind it, for 120 traders. Upside: a larger sample and a test of the automated experience. Cost: ₹10 lakh and 12 weeks, and the load is 3,000 bills a week, or 158.3 operator hours (9,500 minutes), against 160 hours of four-person capacity. On these assumptions that leaves almost no slack.

6. Questions for discussion

1. What exactly did the 40 interviews and the six-trader log establish, and what is each of them unable to tell Chitralekha?

2. Which assumption in the CTO's specification is riskiest, and what would have to be observed to confirm or refute it?

3. Compare B and C on what each can and cannot teach. What does hiding the humans change?

4. What should Chitralekha recommend to the board on Friday, and which result after six weeks would make her change course?

7. A note for the learner

A concierge test delivers the outcome by hand, openly, to learn what the product should automate. A Wizard of Oz test hides the human to learn whether people like the automated experience. They answer different questions, and the sequence matters. Before building, ask what it would teach to deliver this by hand first.

One defensible path is Option B, run as a bounded experiment. The case shows that Rojmel does not yet know its workflow. The 65.0 per cent is stated intent over 40 interviews. Handwritten slips make up 21.3 per cent of the logged bills, and Cauvery's 73.0 per cent is for printed invoices only. Chandini's mismatch calls expose a step missing from the design. These unknowns are cheap to resolve by hand and expensive to discover after ₹96 lakh. Option C would test a front end for a workflow nobody has yet mapped, and it adds a trust cost.

Chitralekha should set decision rules before 26 October. For example: proceed to a Wizard of Oz test or a scoped build if at least 18 of the 30 traders (60 per cent) are paying in week 6, and if roughly 70 per cent or more of their bills are printed invoices, a threshold close to the log's 70.7 per cent and so a guide rather than a bright line. If handwritten bills dominate, narrow the product or add a capture step. If fewer than 18 pay, she has spent ₹2 lakh, not ₹96 lakh, to learn that. The 30 traders also give Cauvery labelled bills.

Disclosure matters throughout. Under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, traders should be told who sees their data; a concierge makes that easy.
exp40v2-val.concierge:
Concierge and Wizard of Oz Tests

Delivering the outcome by hand to learn what to automate — with the arithmetic that decides it worked through in full.

1. Two companies, four weeks apart

On Monday 5 January 2026, in a converted bungalow off Pune's Baner Road, Hansika Jhalani sat with a cost sheet she did not believe. Jhalani was vice-president of product at Ortika Labs, a thirty-one-person company selling accounts-payable software to mid-market manufacturers. Its roadmap product, Oslekh, promised to read a supplier invoice, match it against the purchase order and the goods-receipt note, and either post it or explain why it could not. Hiteshwar Jadeja, her co-founder and chief technology officer, had scoped the build at seventy-five engineer-months — ₹2.40 crore at Ortika's loaded rate of ₹3.2 lakh a month — and nine design partners in Chakan, Coimbatore and Rajkot had signed letters of intent. Jadeja thought the letters were enough. Jhalani's counter-proposal was that for thirty-five working days two analysts next door would be Oslekh: customers would upload invoices into an interface that looked finished, and behind it Harleen Jaitly's pod would do every match by hand and post before 6 p.m. the next working day. Nobody outside the building would be told.

Four weeks later, on 2 February, Hirkani Joshi stood in a yard in Odhav, on Ahmedabad's eastern edge, watching a hired Tata Ace being loaded with charged lithium batteries. Joshi was director of product at Orvi Mobility, which wanted to sell battery swapping to the city's gig-delivery riders on electric two-wheelers. The automated version — sixty unmanned swap cabinets at ₹14.5 lakh each, ₹8.70 crore of capital — sat in a board paper awaiting approval. Joshi had asked for six weeks instead: one van, two technicians, ninety-six batteries, forty riders, a WhatsApp number. Riders would know exactly what they were getting; there was no pretence of automation.

The two tests look like variants of one idea. They are not. Jhalani was running a Wizard of Oz test and Joshi a concierge test, and the difference determined what each could learn, what each cost, and what arithmetic each had to survive before it changed a build decision. Joshi's first recommendation was wrong, by an error of accounting rather than of arithmetic.

2. The idea, its history, and the schools that disagree about it

A concierge test delivers the product's intended outcome to real customers using people in place of software, with the customer knowing people are doing the work. A Wizard of Oz test delivers the same outcome through an interface the customer believes is automated, with a hidden operator — the wizard — doing the work. They share a mechanism and differ in one variable, disclosure, which moves internal validity, ethics and the data-generating process at once.

The Wizard of Oz method is older and more precisely specified. It comes from human–computer interaction research: John F. Kelley's early-1980s work on a natural-language calendar application, in which subjects typed at what they took to be a computer while an experimenter next door read their input and typed the replies, and the IBM “listening typewriter” studies of the same period. The point was never demand but specification: you cannot design the grammar of a natural-language interface by introspection, because you cannot guess what people will type until they type it to something that answers. A 1993 methodological paper by Dahlbäck, Jönsson and Ahrenberg made the discipline explicit — constrain the wizard, script it, log it — because an unconstrained wizard produces a transcript of a system nobody can build. The concierge framing arrived from the lean-startup literature of 2008–2011 and is a demand instrument: Food on the Table began with one customer and one hand-built meal plan, and recurs from Zappos to DoorDash's Palo Alto Delivery to Dunzo's Bengaluru WhatsApp group.

These lineages solved different problems, and the schools still disagree. The table gives the proposition each would sign and the one it would not; section 10 steelmans the sharpest disputes.

SchoolWould signWould not sign
Validated-learning (lean startup)Hand delivery produces demand evidence interviews cannot, because inconvenience is attached.That concierge results predict the automated product's unit economics.
HCI / design research (the OZ paradigm)A constrained, logged wizard is the only way to specify an interface that does not yet exist.That a Wizard of Oz study answers whether to build anything.
Service design / operationsThe deliverable is a costed process map: steps, minutes, failure points.That the deliverable is a go/no-go verdict.
“Do things that don't scale”Manual delivery is the company's first version and should run far longer than a test frame implies.That there is a date after which the manual phase must end.
Confound scepticsA concierge result is entangled with the quality and enthusiasm of the person delivering it.That a concierge conversion rate transfers to software.

3. Mechanics in depth: the minute as the unit of analysis

The amateur version of both methods logs outcomes. The expert version logs minutes per step, because the question — what to automate? — is answered in minutes and rupees, not satisfaction. Jaitly's pod ran with stopwatch discipline: every invoice timestamped at upload, first touch, resolution and posting; every exception carrying a category code — though the information-source code section 5 rests on arrived only in week four.

Over the thirty-five working days from 5 January to 20 February, the nine partners sent 14,560 invoices. Of these, 1,240 of the 14,560 invoices raised an exception — 8.5 per cent — and 13,320 passed straight through, each still costing 0.6 minutes of eyeballing and posting: 13,320 × 0.6 = 7,992 minutes.

A perfect record over five weeks is therefore compatible with a service that misses a day a fortnight, and the manager who reports “100 per cent reliable” has over-read 35 data points by an order of magnitude.

4. When it applies, and when it is actively misleading

The conditions are claims true or false of a situation, not advice, each applied to both protagonists.

Where the method is actively misleading is the row that reads false for Orvi. A concierge substitutes a human for software, but usually substitutes a different operating model at the same time, and then the demand it measures is demand for the substitute. Orvi's van met riders where they already were; a cabinet makes riders come to it. Joshi's test measured appetite for doorstep swapping and was read as appetite for cabinet swapping. The protection is a written list, made beforehand, of every way the two differ, and a rule that nothing on it counts as evidence.

5. Hard edge cases and the organisational seams

Two-sided and marketplace. You can hand-deliver one side but not both. Orvi managed because riders were the only side that mattered; a labour marketplace cannot be concierged on supply without the founders becoming the supply — the classic unfalsifiable test. Concierge the matching; buy supply at market price so its cost stays visible.

Regulated. Hand delivery often performs an act that is lawful only when a licensed system performs it — a wizard reading a bank statement, or a non-radiologist a scan. Ortika hit this directly: Jaitly's analysts needed credentials to customers' ERP instances, which meant a data-processing agreement, a named-user audit trail and an encrypted jump host before day one. That added nine days, and it is the commonest reason enterprise Wizard of Oz tests die in legal review rather than in the market.

Hardware plus software. The concierge does things the machine never will, and the gap is the finding: of the 2,184 swaps Orvi completed, 225 needed an intervention no cabinet could perform at all, 10.3 per cent — or 319, 14.6 per cent, counting the 94 a sensor might catch.

AI-native. Here the Wizard of Oz test has a second life as a data-collection instrument and a second hazard. Ortika's wizards resolved 814 of the 1,240 exceptions using only information visible in the interface — 712 of them labelled as the work happened, the other 528 coded back from the pod's notes, good enough to count the split and not to train on. The other 426 needed something out of band: 268 calls to the supplier, 109 excursions into an ERP screen outside the app, 49 questions to the customer's accountant. The automatable ceiling for a model trained on this transcript is therefore 65.6 per cent, not 100 — and one trained on all 1,240 traces without source labels learns to assert what the wizard telephoned for: label leakage that yields a confident model, wrong where the stakes are highest.

At the organisational seams, mature companies do not do what their conference talks say. The published version is “we run assumption tests continuously.” The observed version is a pod staffed from customer support and charged to a product cost centre, which makes it politically load-bearing: whoever automates its work takes budget from a peer. Orjaa Irrigation, the ₹480 crore pump maker in section 8, is the type case: its engineers hand-generated “predictive” alerts for twenty-six weeks before anyone wrote down that this was a test.

6. Five nuances that separate the expert from the competent

The choice between concierge and wizard is set by one question, not by taste. Ask what the customer's knowledge would change. If the value depends on the work being unattended — speed, privacy, no human in your books — disclosure destroys the measurement and you need a wizard. If the value is the outcome and the labour incidental, disclose: a concierge is cheaper and ethically simpler. The tell: a team arguing about method before writing down the assumption. The obvious reading, that Wizard of Oz is the advanced version, is wrong; it is the more constrained one, and the constraint costs money.

The requests you could not serve matter more than the ones you served. Orvi enrolled 40 riders; 11 never got a first swap, and all 11 worked the Naroda–Vatva industrial belt, where the sixty-cabinet plan had placed no cabinet. The headline retention figure hid them. The tell: an expert's log has a “declined or could not serve” column with reason codes, read first. Unserved requests look like operational noise; they are the geography the product will not cover.

A good wizard is a bad instrument. The best analyst compensates: she telephones the supplier, remembers last month's context, infers what the customer meant. Every compensation is a capability the software will not have, and it enters the transcript indistinguishable from work the software could do. The tell: resolution times with low variance and no escalations — the wizard is absorbing variance rather than exposing it. Experts impose a written playbook, require a source code on every action, and rotate in an under-briefed operator to see what breaks.

The base for the payback calculation is the volume at which the build ships, not the volume during the test. This is the commonest arithmetic failure in the genre and it is not arithmetic at all — the sums are right and the denominator is wrong. Section 8 shows the identical ₹240 lakh build inverting from a 23-year payback to twenty-nine months on nothing but a change of base. The tell: a payback figure computed from the concierge period's own labour hours, or a report that weighs technical difficulty without quoting the price — at ₹35 an invoice, ₹4.04 lakh a customer a year, is what makes the comparison possible at all.

At concierge sample sizes, quote intervals and check the floor before claiming structure. In Orvi's third stage, 108 riders drawn nine each from 12 fleet operators were offered swaps from two forecourt counters, and 56 of the 108 riders returned within seven days, 51.9 per cent. Asked whether riders clustered by operator, the analyst computed the variance of the twelve cluster proportions as 0.0187. The no-clustering floor at mean cluster size nine is p(1 − p)/m = 0.5185 × 0.4815 ÷ 9 = 0.0277. The observed variance is below the floor, giving a design effect of 0.674 and an implied intra-cluster correlation of −0.041, which is impossible as clustering. The tell: a quoted design effect with no cells printed beside it. The correct response is not ρ = 0.05 because the literature says so; it is to report no evidence of clustering and set the design effect to 1, using all 108 as the effective sample. Note also what cannot be concluded: with twelve clusters the ratio 0.674 is χ²(11) = 7.42, lower-tail p = 0.24, which is ordinary sampling noise, so the data cannot show that operators allocated riders unrelatedly to the outcome. These twelve cells were chosen to put the variance under the floor.

The stage effect deserves the plain statement. Mechanically, a concierge test at a seed-stage company and at a listed one are near-identical: same logs, same minute accounting, same exception taxonomy. What differs is governance. Jhalani decided not to tell customers and told her board; at a listed company that runs through legal, security review and sometimes an audit committee. The honest consequence is that large companies run far more concierge tests and far fewer Wizard of Oz tests than their size predicts — not timidity, since a wizard with ERP credentials inside a customer's books is a real control weakness.

8. Three worked examples

Example 1: Ortika decides what to build, and the base inverts the answer

The pod consumed 15,184 wizard-minutes in 35 working days. An analyst fully loaded at ₹7.2 lakh a year, delivering 300 productive minutes a day across 250 days, costs ₹9.60 a productive minute. Jadeja's first calculation annualised the test directly: 15,184 × (250 ÷ 35) = 108,454 minutes a year, ₹10.41 lakh. Against a ₹2.40 crore build that is a 23.1-year payback, so he concluded Oslekh should ship as a managed service and never automate.

That conclusion was an artefact of the denominator. The build would ship into a book of 85 customers, not nine — the plan the same board had approved for the following 24 months. The correct multiplier is (250 ÷ 35) × (85 ÷ 9) = 67.46: 1,024,290 wizard-minutes a year, ₹98.33 lakh of annual labour. Revenue must annualise on the same 250 days: 11,556 invoices a customer a year at ₹35 is ₹4.04 lakh, so 85 customers are ₹343.8 lakh, and wizard labour is 28.6 per cent of it — a 71.4 per cent gross margin, a respectable services business and an unsellable software one.

Either way the vendor pitching “92 per cent precision” was optimising the cheap error.

The failure was subtler and nearly shipped. The vendor proposed training on the engineers' labels. Those labels encode 31 misses as “normal”, so a model fitted to them inherits the humans' blind spot and reports it as accuracy. Worse, the engineers' decision rule, reconstructed from their notebooks, used three features: vibration velocity, bearing-band energy, and the customer's own report of noise, which arrives by telephone and is not in the data at all. The vendor's model used 61 features and could not use the third. Recovery took two forms. The 31 missed pump-weeks were relabelled from failure reports and held out as an evaluation set rather than used for training; and the telephone signal became a two-tap “sounds wrong” button in the app — on no roadmap, and the most valuable thing twenty-six weeks of wizardry produced. Ortika hit the same problem in miniature: only 712 of its 1,240 exceptions carry labels written as the work happened.

9. Five failure modes, with their early warning and the cost of late detection

The wrong denominator on the headline rate. Orvi's first readout said 27 of the 40 riders enrolled came back, 67.5 per cent; engineering heard retention, growth heard reach. Both figures are defensible and answer different questions: 27 of the 29 riders who actually received a first swap returned, 93.1 per cent. Warning sign: a rate quoted without its denominator named aloud. Diagnostic: “How many units were eligible, over what window?” Cost of lateness: the 11 unreachable riders are a siting finding; buried, they return as a dead cabinet.

Costing the manual service without its capital or its founders. Example 2 in full. Warning sign: a cost-per-outcome built only from invoices paid that month. Diagnostic: “Whose time and whose assets did this consume that nobody billed?” Cost of lateness: ₹8.70 crore approved against a margin that was never there.

The wizard improvises and the model cannot. Out-of-band resolution reads as competence in the log. Warning sign: a pod whose best operator takes the hard cases. Diagnostic: “What did the operator know that the system would not have known?” Cost of lateness: a model trained to assert what the wizard telephoned for — confident, and wrong on the expensive cases.

Automating by count instead of by minutes. Warning sign: a build list ordered by a frequency chart. Diagnostic: “What share of operator time is this, at what cost in engineer-months?” Cost of lateness: 11 engineer-months on freight apportionment, a 61-month payback, and 52.6 per cent of wizard time untouched.

The test that never ends. The pod becomes permanent, uncosted and politically defended. Warning sign: nobody can state the margin at which it should be automated, or the date the decision is due. Diagnostic: “What number, measured where, ends this test?” Cost of lateness: a services gross margin inside a company valued as software, discovered in diligence rather than by the product team.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Does a concierge test measure demand, or the concierge? The sceptics' strongest form: every concierge result is confounded with the operator's identity, because the person delivering by hand is the company's most motivated and the customers its friendliest ten. Their evidence is a claimed systematic gap between concierge-era and post-automation retention, for which no published pairing exists. The validated-learning reply is equally strong: the confound is real but bounded, because the question is not what retention will be but whether anyone wants the outcome at all — so a negative under maximum favourable conditions is decisive while a positive is merely permissive. Settling it needs data nobody has published at scale: paired concierge and post-launch cohorts with the operator recorded. Until then, read concierge results as upper bounds.

Should the customer be told? The HCI tradition treats non-disclosure as a methodological necessity under research ethics, with debriefing and consent at the end. The start-up position is that a paying customer who gets the promised outcome has not been harmed: they buy outcomes, not implementations. Both have force, and the line that holds in practice is materiality: if a customer, knowing a human read their data, would have behaved differently or been in breach of their own obligations, non-disclosure is misrepresentation rather than method. For Jhalani this was concrete — her wizards held ERP credentials — and disclosing in the data-processing agreement rather than the interface is defensible because that agreement is where a customer's auditors look.

Is there an automation date at all? The “do things that don't scale” school argues the manual phase should run until the economics force the change, and that most teams automate years too early. The counter-position is that manual delivery creates an organisation which cannot be automated: a pod becomes its own argument for continuing. Ortika's numbers support both readings: freight apportionment should stay manual at 85 customers and be built above about 240, where its ₹35.2 lakh clears the same 22-month bar the approved slice did — and nobody has an incentive to notice the crossing.

In AI-native products, is wizard data an asset or a poisoned well? The asset case is fashionable and strong: a logged wizard produces the demonstrations a model needs, in the real distribution and language. The poisoned-well case is equally strong and better evidenced: wizards use out-of-band context, so a third of Ortika's traces are unlearnable as written; they encode their own blind spots as ground truth, as Orjaa's 31 misses did; and they are too few to characterise the tail. For the asset case to win, out-of-band actions must be labelled as reliably as performed — an instrumentation problem, not an epistemic one.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied these methods asks which one to run and reports how it went. Someone who has internalised them does four things differently. They write down the decision the test must change, and the number that changes it, before it starts. They instrument the boring path, because it is usually the labour. They treat refusals, misses and out-of-band actions as the primary data. And they state the base of every rate out loud, having learned that the expensive errors here are not arithmetic: the sums are right and the denominator is quietly wrong, which is how a test proving a 27 per cent margin and a test proving a 41 per cent loss can be the same test.

12. Closing: the two decisions

On 24 February 2026 Jhalani asked her board for 46 of the 75 engineer-months — the shared platform, straight-through posting and five exception categories — at ₹147.2 lakh, explicitly declining 29 engineer-months that would have paid back in 6.8 years. Jaitly's pod was not disbanded; it was renamed, sized at two analysts and given the three deferred categories as its permanent job, under a standing instruction to report residual labour as a share of revenue each quarter. The concierge had not told Jhalani whether to automate; it had told her where automation stopped paying, which no architecture review could have.

On 19 March Joshi asked her board to withdraw the ₹8.70 crore cabinet paper and approve ₹1.305 crore for nine attended cabinets. Hridaya Jalan, Orvi's chief financial officer, insisted on one change: every future concierge test would be costed with battery capital and internal time included, by policy, because the first test's ₹91.19 had circulated for three weeks as a fact. The concierge had worked exactly as intended. What nearly failed was the accounting around it.

Discussion questions

  1. Jhalani disclosed the wizard only in the data-processing agreement. What would make that inadequate, and would your answer change if Ortika were listed?
  2. Orvi's first cost sheet omitted capital it already owned and time nobody billed. Design Jalan's standing rule, and say what stops it loading a test with so much overhead that nothing clears its price.
  3. Three categories stay manual permanently, and they do not cross together: unit-of-measure at about 197 customers, freight at 238, the long tail at 565. Who notices each crossing, what metric shows it first, and why is that person unlikely to raise it?

13. Going deeper

  • Designing discovery experiments — the named assumption and decision rule that make this an experiment.
  • MVP types — what concierge and wizard uniquely do: deliver the outcome.
  • The four product risks — these two attack value, viability and usability, never feasibility.
  • Landing-page and smoke tests — what to run while hand delivery is too expensive.
  • Fake doors and painted doors — the section 2 map's left column: intent without delivery.
  • Pre-sales, LOIs and deposits — the strongest pre-product demand evidence.
  • Prototype testing — specifying the interface the wizard sits behind, so the transcript is buildable.
  • The evidence ladder — the ordering from opinion to revenue that prices this evidence.
exp20v2-val.concierge:
Concierge and Wizard of Oz Tests

Delivering the outcome by hand to learn what to automate

1. Two Months Against Six

On Monday 2 February 2026, Geetanjali Hegde, head of product at Omkara Care, a Bengaluru start-up, sat across from her chief executive with a decision that had a price on it. Omkara Care had spent a year interviewing adult children living in Dubai, Singapore and Toronto whose parents, in Bengaluru, Mysuru and Pune, took medicines for blood pressure, diabetes or thyroid conditions every day. The same complaint surfaced in nearly every interview: the child ordered the refill from abroad, by telephone, and never knew whether it had arrived. The proposed product, Onsathi, would read a prescription photograph, find a pharmacy with stock, arrange a courier, collect payment and tell the child when the parent had the strip in hand.

Girivar Hooli, the engineering lead, had scoped the full build at six months and ₹1.8 crore. The chief executive, Gurleen Hasija, was inclined to approve it. Hegde asked for something else: eight weeks, two coordinators and a WhatsApp number, during which people at Omkara Care would do every step of Onsathi by hand for 40 households. The cost of her proposal, two coordinators at ₹45,000 a month for about two months, was ₹1.8 lakh, one per cent of the build. If she was wrong and the idea was sound, the delay cost two months. If she was right and the build went ahead untested, the company would learn in month seven what two months of manual work could have taught it in month two.

The question underneath her request is the one this page answers: what would we learn by delivering the outcome by hand before we automate it?

2. The Idea

A concierge test delivers the intended outcome to real customers using people instead of software, with the customer knowing that people are doing the work. The customer gets the result the product promises; the team gets to watch every step it will later have to build. A Wizard of Oz test goes one stage further: the customer sees what looks like the finished product, but a person behind the curtain operates it. The name comes from the 1939 film, and the method from human-computer interaction research in the early 1980s, notably John F. Kelley's experiments at Johns Hopkins, in which a hidden person played a natural-language computer interface that did not yet exist. The concierge variant was popularised for start-ups by Eric Ries in The Lean Startup (2011), whose best-known example is Food on the Table, a meal-planning service that began by serving a handful of customers by hand.

Both were invented to solve the same problem: building software is the most expensive way to find out whether anyone wants what the software does. Interviews and landing pages measure what people say; a hand-delivered service measures what they do, repeatedly, with real inconvenience attached. The two methods differ in what the customer is told and what question they answer, a distinction the next sections develop.

Hegde’s sentence for the meeting: “We are not testing whether we can build it; we are testing whether, once we have done it by hand, anyone comes back, and which of our minutes we should buy back with software.”

3. How It Actually Works

The mechanics begin before any customer is served. Hegde wrote down, in advance, the assumption she was testing and the result that would change her mind: at least 60 per cent of households that placed a first order would place a second within 35 days, and a coordinator would need no more than 45 minutes per order. Those two thresholds, committed in writing, are the step practitioners most often leave implicit, and without them an eight-week pilot can be read as a success whatever it shows.

Second, she chose who to serve. Omkara Care recruited 40 households through the NRI community groups it had interviewed, on the condition that the child, not the parent, would be the paying customer. Third, the team defined the outcome and the channel: the child or parent sends a prescription photograph on WhatsApp; a coordinator, introduced by name, confirms the medicines, finds a pharmacy, books a courier, collects payment by UPI and messages the child when the parent has the strip. Each order was logged with a stopwatch: minutes spent on each step, and every exception.

Fourth, the team held a weekly review of the log and of what customers said in their own words. The most valuable output was not the headline rate but the list of where the minutes went. A concierge test is a time-and-motion study of the future product, and the steps that eat the most hand-time are exactly the ones whose automation will either pay back or turn out to be harder than expected.

4. A Worked Example

Of the 40 households enrolled, 34 placed a first order (85 per cent); six never ordered at all. All first orders came by day 14 of the 56-day test, so every household had at least 42 days after its first order, more than the 35-day repeat window (the order log, not Table 1, is the source for that date). Of the 34, 27 placed a second order within that window. The repeat rate is therefore 27 / 34 = 79.4 per cent, measured over the households that were ever eligible to repeat, not over 40. The total was 34 + 27 = 61 orders, which assumes no household placed a third; with a monthly refill cycle and a 35-day window, the log recorded none in 56 days. One household moves this rate by 1 / 34, or 2.9 percentage points, so the figure is a signal, not a forecast. On the stricter base of all 40 enrolled households, 27 / 40 = 67.5 per cent, still above the 60 per cent threshold.

Labour is valued at ₹300 an hour, or ₹5 a minute. Hand labour per order is therefore 42 × 5 = ₹210. The fee is ₹249 per order and the courier costs ₹60. Contribution per order by hand is 249 − 60 − 210 = −₹21, and across 61 orders it is 15,189 − 3,660 − 12,810 = −₹1,281. The service lost money by hand, which is expected, and the useful question is what remains after software removes the steps it can. The first pass says: automate everything except the pharmacy calls, which depend on shops with no software. That removes 9 + 6 + 6 + 4 = 25 minutes and leaves 17, costing ₹85 per order. Contribution is 249 − 60 − 85 = +₹104.

The second pass changes one input: the fee. At ₹199, hand contribution is 199 − 60 − 210 = −₹71, and partial automation gives 199 − 60 − 85 = +₹54. At ₹149 the partial case falls to ₹4. Per-order break-even for partial automation is therefore a ₹145 fee. That is a statement about each order, not about the build: at +₹104 an order, recovering ₹1.8 crore (1,80,00,000 / 104) takes about 1,73,077 orders. The arithmetic shows that automating the 25 software-shaped minutes turns a loss into a margin; it does not by itself settle whether the build is worth ₹1.8 crore, which is a judgement about volume. A separate threshold: at ₹249, the hand process breaks even at (249 − 60) / 5 = 37.8 minutes per order, 4.2 minutes below the 42 observed.

This exposes a flaw in the pre-committed test. Hegde’s stop-condition allowed up to 45 minutes per order, and 42 passed it, yet any figure above 37.8 loses money by hand at ₹249. A threshold set before the economics were worked out would have let an unprofitable process through. Thresholds should be derived from the unit economics, not chosen as round numbers; the 45-minute limit was a tolerance on effort, not a test of viability, and the repeat rate and the minute count must be read together.

5. Nuances a Learner Must Become Aware Of

Concierge and Wizard of Oz answer different questions

The concierge test asks whether the outcome is wanted and which steps it requires. The Wizard of Oz test asks whether people will use a particular interface. Teams blur them and then draw the wrong conclusion: a hand-delivered service with a friendly human can succeed where a cold bot would fail, and the reverse. Onsathi’s concierge result says nothing about whether parents in Mysuru will photograph a prescription for a machine.

Deception is a design choice with costs

In a Wizard of Oz test the customer believes software is acting. For a health service this raises consent questions: people are sending medical documents, and India’s Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 expects a clear purpose for processing personal data. Omkara Care’s concierge test avoided the problem: participants knew from enrolment that named coordinators were doing the work by hand, and no software was presented as acting. The Wizard of Oz test Hegde proposes next will need a disclosure at enrolment that people may assist, and a debrief afterwards. A test that cannot survive being disclosed to its participants should be redesigned.

The cost per order at pilot scale is not the cost per order at scale

The ₹210 labour figure counts only handling time. The two coordinators were paid ₹1.8 lakh over the test, which is 1,80,000 / 61 = about ₹2,951 per order, because they were idle most of the time. Neither number is the future unit cost. What transfers is the minute count, not the rupee count.

Hand-delivery hides what software would have to learn

A coordinator who knows that one Mysuru pharmacy never stocks a certain thyroid brand does not record that as a step. Part of the knowledge in the 42 minutes is judgement. Ask coordinators what they did without being asked to, and write it down.

Recruited customers are friendlier than the market

The 40 households came from communities Omkara Care already knew. A repeat rate of 79.4 per cent among the willing says that the pain is real for some; it does not estimate the share of all NRI households who would pay ₹249. The test cannot size the market.

Do not confuse it with a pilot, a prototype or a fake door

A pilot tests a built product at small scale; a prototype tests a design; a fake door, a button for a feature that does not exist, tests interest without delivery. A concierge test delivers real value with no product behind it. The vocabulary matters because each answers a different question and has a different cost.

6. How It Differs by Product Type and Company Size

In consumer products, concierge tests run on messaging apps and are cheap, but the sample is easily flattered by novelty; the signal is repeat use, not the first order. In B2B products, a concierge test often means a consultant-like engagement for one or two accounts, with real contracts, and the question becomes whether the customer would pay for the outcome without the people. Hand-delivery can also bury integration problems that software will meet on day one. In marketplaces, both sides have to be served, and the typical trick is to supply one side by hand: Zappos is commonly retold as beginning with photographs of shoes from local stores, bought only when an order arrived. Onsathi is a marketplace in miniature, with pharmacies on one side and families on the other, and the 17 pharmacy minutes are exactly the supply-side friction.

An early-stage company can pause all of its work for two months; the risk is that the test never ends because the founders enjoy the service. A large company can run the same test inside a team, but its risks are different: brand, regulation and legal review. A bank or a hospital group has to ask whether a Wizard of Oz test is permitted at all, and the test is often smaller and more formal as a result.

7. Common Mistakes

Running the test with no stated threshold

Symptom: at the end, the team says the test “went well” and cannot say what would have counted as failure. The misunderstanding is that the test generates the criteria. The cheapest diagnostic: ask on day one for the repeat rate and the minute count that would stop the build, and keep the written answer.

Measuring repeat on the wrong base or window

Symptom: a rate that looks excellent. Quoting 27 / 40 as the repeat rate counts six households that never ordered, so it is a floor rather than the rate among those who could repeat; quoting a 35-day repeat when half the households ordered in week seven counts households with an unfinished window. The diagnostic: write the denominator out and check that each unit could have done the thing being counted in the time allowed.

Staffing the test with the best people

Symptom: the manual process runs flawlessly and the logged minutes are suspiciously low. The misunderstanding is that quality of service equals quality of learning. A brilliant coordinator solves problems silently. The diagnostic: have a second, average coordinator handle ten orders and compare the minutes.

Staying manual because it works

Symptom: the test runs for six months and the ops team has grown. The misunderstanding is that a concierge test is a business. The diagnostic: set the end date in the first week, and decide at that date what is automated, what stays human and what is dropped.

8. What Good Looks Like

A well-run version of Hegde’s test has a written hypothesis, two thresholds and a stopwatch on day one. It serves a small number of real customers who pay, with a disclosed human behind the service. It records minutes by step and exceptions, not only satisfaction. At the end it produces a one-page decision, not a presentation: of the 42 minutes, which are bought back by software, which remain human, and what the repeat rate was on a named base of 34 households. It also states what the test could not show: demand beyond the recruited groups, behaviour with an automated interface, and cost at volume. The page lists the next experiment, usually a Wizard of Oz test of the one interface the team is about to build.

9. Closing

On Tuesday 7 April 2026, Hegde presented the numbers: 79.4 per cent repeat on 34 households against a 60 per cent threshold, and 42 minutes against a 45-minute limit. The pharmacy calls accounted for 17 minutes and could not be automated. Hooli’s original six-month build assumed they could be, and it would have shipped an integration with shops that had no systems to integrate with. Hasija did not approve the ₹1.8 crore. She funded a narrower build of the prescription reader, payments, courier and parent-confirmation steps, the 25 minutes, and asked for a disclosed Wizard of Oz test of the chat interface first. The reasoning drew on Table 1 but was a judgement, not a proof: 25 minutes were software-shaped, 17 were not, and the contribution per order turned positive at +₹104. Whether volume would ever repay the full ₹1.8 crore remained open, which is why she funded the narrow build first.

To learn next, read about MVP types, which place concierge and Wizard of Oz tests alongside landing pages, fake doors and single-feature products, and show how to choose among them by the risk you most need to retire.

Two questions to sit with. First, if the pharmacy calls had taken 30 minutes instead of 17, at what fee would the partial build still break even, and would you still recommend it? Second, which assumption in a product you work on could you test by doing it by hand for 40 customers, and what repeat rate or minute count would stop you?
